chunk_findings.detail:
`_fit_sections` does not guarantee its result fits in `room`. `allow[i]` is `min(size_i, max(int(room * share), _SECTION_FLOOR))`, and because `_SECTION_FLOOR = 160` is a floor, `sum(allow)` can exceed `room` (the nine shares sum to 1.0, but four small-share sections get bumped up to 160). When that happens `slack = room - sum(allow)` is negative, the `while slack > 0` loop never runs, no allowance is ever reduced, and every section for which `size <= allow` is emitted in full while `trimmed` stays `False`. The budget is therefore silently exceeded exactly in the case this change is meant to police.

Concrete repro at the default budget converted to characters (room = 4800): section sizes of recovery 480, jobs 240, current 960, ready 576, decisions 1200, memories 384, rules 160, lessons 720, skills 160. Their sum is 4880 > 4800, so the early `sum(sizes) <= room` return does not fire. Each size equals its computed allowance (`decisions` 0.25*4800=1200, `rules` max(96,160)=160, `skills` max(144,160)=160, …), so `allow = sizes`, `sum(allow)=4880`, `slack=-80`; the loop is skipped, all sections satisfy `size <= room_i`, and the function returns 4880 characters with `trimmed=False`. A caller that trusts `trimmed` to add the "cut to fit" note will not add it, and the brief is 80 characters over budget. The error grows with smaller configured budgets: with room = 1000 the allowances sum to 1680 (`recovery`→160, `jobs`→160, `ready`→160, `memories`→160, `rules`→160, `skills`→160 vs. their 100–144 proportional shares), and a brief whose sections each sit at or below their allowance is returned essentially untrimmed (e.g. nine 150-character sections = 1350 characters against a 1000-character room, `trimmed=False`). The distribution loop assumes `sum(allow) < room`; whenever the floors push the sum over `room` it never trims anything and `trimmed` misreports the result.

chunk_findings.detail: The backstop's *slice* reserves space for the trailing note (`text[: budget * 4 - len(note)]`), but its *trigger* does not: it tests `_approx_tokens(text)` while `text` is still `"\n".join(head + body)`, i.e. before the note is appended. Since `room` handed to `_fit_sections` already subtracts `len(note)`, the only circumstance in which the backstop can fire is the one the code's own comment acknowledges ("a heading alone overran its share"). In exactly that case, if the overrun `delta` is less than `len(note)` (~105 chars at the default token size), `len(text)` stays under `budget*4`, the check is False, `trimmed` is still True from `_fit_sections`, and `text += note` then pushes the result past the cap. Concrete input: `session.brief_max_tokens = 1200` (so `budget*4 = 4800`, `len(note) ~= 105`); `_fit_sections` returns `head + body` of 4770 chars (it overran the 4679-char `room` by 90 because a section's heading/first line would not shrink further); `_approx_tokens(4770) = 1192 <= 1200`, so no truncation runs and the 105-char note is appended, producing ~4875 chars ≈ 1218 tokens — over the 1200-token budget the docstring promises ("The session-start pack, under `session.brief_max_tokens`"). The trigger must account for the note too (e.g. test after appending, or compare against `budget - len(note)//4`).

Under that rule these 20 jobs are the requesting agent's own jobs and must be printed in full, but `test_trimmed_sections_say_where_the_rest_is` asserts `"Jother000" not in text` and expects `f"{JOBS} more unended job(s)"` plus `"ddflow job list"` in the brief. The demonstration input is exactly `_project()`: agent `a1` owns `Jother000..Jother019`, and the brief is fetched with `agent="a1"`, so `Jother000` appears in full and the summary count is not 20. To actually exercise summarisation the non-requested jobs must be recorded under a different agent id (or the ownership check must be by item, which contradicts the stated fix).

chunk_findings.detail:
`_fit_sections` does not guarantee its result fits in `room`. `allow[i]` is `min(size_i, max(int(room * share), _SECTION_FLOOR))`, and because `_SECTION_FLOOR = 160` is a floor, `sum(allow)` can exceed `room` (the nine shares sum to 1.0, but four small-share sections get bumped up to 160). When that happens `slack = room - sum(allow)` is negative, the `while slack > 0` loop never runs, no allowance is ever reduced, and every section for which `size <= allow` is emitted in full while `trimmed` stays `False`. The budget is therefore silently exceeded exactly in the case this change is meant to police.

Concrete repro at the default budget converted to characters (room = 4800): section sizes of recovery 480, jobs 240, current 960, ready 576, decisions 1200, memories 384, rules 160, lessons 720, skills 160. Their sum is 4880 > 4800, so the early `sum(sizes) <= room` return does not fire. Each size equals its computed allowance (`decisions` 0.25*4800=1200, `rules` max(96,160)=160, `skills` max(144,160)=160, …), so `allow = sizes`, `sum(allow)=4880`, `slack=-80`; the loop is skipped, all sections satisfy `size <= room_i`, and the function returns 4880 characters with `trimmed=False`. A caller that trusts `trimmed` to add the "cut to fit" note will not add it, and the brief is 80 characters over budget. The error grows with smaller configured budgets: with room = 1000 the allowances sum to 1680 (`recovery`→160, `jobs`→160, `ready`→160, `memories`→160, `rules`→160, `skills`→160 vs. their 100–144 proportional shares), and a brief whose sections each sit at or below their allowance is returned essentially untrimmed (e.g. nine 150-character sections = 1350 characters against a 1000-character room, `trimmed=False`). The distribution loop assumes `sum(allow) < room`; whenever the floors push the sum over `room` it never trims anything and `trimmed` misreports the result.

chunk_findings.detail: The backstop's *slice* reserves space for the trailing note (`text[: budget * 4 - len(note)]`), but its *trigger* does not: it tests `_approx_tokens(text)` while `text` is still `"\n".join(head + body)`, i.e. before the note is appended. Since `room` handed to `_fit_sections` already subtracts `len(note)`, the only circumstance in which the backstop can fire is the one the code's own comment acknowledges ("a heading alone overran its share"). In exactly that case, if the overrun `delta` is less than `len(note)` (~105 chars at the default token size), `len(text)` stays under `budget*4`, the check is False, `trimmed` is still True from `_fit_sections`, and `text += note` then pushes the result past the cap. Concrete input: `session.brief_max_tokens = 1200` (so `budget*4 = 4800`, `len(note) ~= 105`); `_fit_sections` returns `head + body` of 4770 chars (it overran the 4679-char `room` by 90 because a section's heading/first line would not shrink further); `_approx_tokens(4770) = 1192 <= 1200`, so no truncation runs and the 105-char note is appended, producing ~4875 chars ≈ 1218 tokens — over the 1200-token budget the docstring promises ("The session-start pack, under `session.brief_max_tokens`"). The trigger must account for the note too (e.g. test after appending, or compare against `budget - len(note)//4`).

chunk_findings.detail: `_SECTION_FLOOR` is no longer a floor. The initial allowance is now `min(size, int(room * share))` for every section, and the floor is only topped up out of `slack = room - sum(allow)`. Whenever the sections still want their shares, `slack` is only the truncation remainder of `room * share` (at most ~1 char per section), while the shortfall for a section whose floor exceeds its share is `_SECTION_FLOOR - int(room * share)`. Concretely, with `room = 4000`, six sections sharing .35/.25/.20/.10/.05/.05 and `_SECTION_FLOOR = 300`: the two 5% sections are allowed `int(4000*0.05) = 200`, i.e. 100 chars under their floor, but `slack <= 6`, so the top-up loop (`extra = max(0, min(slack, min(size, _SECTION_FLOOR) - allow[i]))`) hands them a few characters at most and they are trimmed below the floor. If those sections are "rules"/"lessons", the trailing rule/lesson lines disappear — the exact failure this change is supposed to guarantee against. The named regression test does not catch it, because the now-collapsed jobs section is tiny and leaves enough slack for the floors to be met.

chunk_findings.detail: `lease_taken_over_by` returns the *first* displaced entry matching `event` + `acquired_at`, but the displaced record is explicitly uncapped ("every displaced claim (no cap)") and this feature itself is what makes a claim displaceable more than once. `_redisplay` promotes a taken-over contestant without removing its `displaced` entry (it only calls `_hold`), so the same claim window can appear on `displaced` multiple times, once per takeover. Concretely: (1) C's claim is taken over by H1, so `displaced` gets `{event: C.event, lease: C, by: H1}`; H1 releases → `_redisplay` shows C, correctly marked `taken_over_by = H1`. (2) Later C's claim lapses again and is taken over by H2, appending `{event: C.event, lease: C, by: H2}`; H2 releases → `_redisplay` shows C again, but the loop hits the H1 entry first and returns `H1`. `show`/`status --json` then report "previously taken over by H1" even though the redisplay was caused by H2's release, and the current taker (H2) is omitted. The marker should be derived from the most recent matching displacement (e.g. newest matching entry), not the first one encountered in `self.displaced`.

The cross-kind refusal is suppressed with `chk = _cross_kind(repo, rule, agent, DD.Answer("new") if answer else None)`, i.e. on the mere truthiness of `answer`, but the docstring states the rule is filed "unless it reads like a record of another kind and nobody has answered `new`". Nothing here re-checks `answer.relation` (and, unlike `_points_elsewhere`, nothing re-checks `answer.problem`), so any non-`None` `RuleDedupAnswer` is turned into the user having said "new".

Concrete inputs:
- A problem-flagged answer (the CLI/MCP mis-parses an answer, e.g. `RuleDedupAnswer(relation="extend", target="rule-999", problem="unknown target")`). `_points_elsewhere` returns `False` because it guards on `not answer.problem`, execution falls through to `_add_checked_against_others`, `answer` is truthy, `DD.Answer("new")` is handed to `check_add`, no refusal is returned, and the rule is written to disk even though its text restates an existing decision — the very refusal the change is supposed to surface is silently skipped and the malformed answer is treated as approval.
- An answer whose `relation` is `"related"` but whose `target` is an existing *rule* (so `_points_elsewhere` is `False` via `not _is_rule`). Since the rule-level prompt is a separate check (`rule_dedup_check`, per `_cross_kind`'s docstring) the other-kind candidate was never shown to the user, yet `_add_checked_against_others` again substitutes `Answer("new")` and files the rule without ever running the decision/lesson/task comparison.

The suppression should be conditioned on `answer.relation == "new"` (and no `answer.problem`), not on `answer` being non-empty.

chunk_findings.detail: Given an environment where an existing rule R1 and an existing decision D are both similar to a new rule R2, the two entry points return different verdicts. `rule check R2` unconditionally invokes `_cross_kind`, merges D's candidate (kind "decision") and sets `would_ask=True`, even though the rule-vs-rule dedupe already produced `is_duplicate=True` with R1 as a candidate. `rule add R2` with no `dedup_answer` takes `is_duplicate=True`, so the new guard `not is_duplicate and (...)` is false, the cross-kind call is never made, and the add flow goes to the pre-existing rule-duplicate branch. The user answers "new" for R1; on re-entry `is_duplicate` is still true (R1 still exists) and `dedup_answer.relation == "new"` cannot rescue the guard because it also requires `not is_duplicate`, so `_add_checked_against_others` is never reached and D is never surfaced. The check therefore reports a candidate/would-ask that the add path can never produce (the inverse of the comment "as `rule add` would meet it"), and the D-rule-dedupe-everywhere goal is silently skipped for any rule that also duplicates another rule. Either the check should be gated on `not is_duplicate` to match add, or the add path's cross-kind check must also run in the rule-duplicate branch before finalizing a "new" answer; the two paths in this diff do not agree.

chunk_findings.detail: The MCP edit tool resolves the dedup answer with `RuleDedupAnswer("new", "") if bool(a.get("new")) else (RuleDedupAnswer("related", a["related"]) if a.get("related") else None)`. There is no schema-level exclusivity: `"new": ("boolean", ...)` and `"related": ("string", ...)` are declared as independent optional properties, and the schema format used here cannot express "at most one of". So a client that sends `{"id": "R1", "content": "...", "new": true, "related": "T42"}` (legal under the declared schema) silently gets `RuleDedupAnswer("new", "")`: the explicit `related` answer is dropped and the edit is treated as a brand-new record. The equivalent CLI invocation `rule edit --new --related T42` fails with an argparse "not allowed with argument" error, so the two surfaces disagree on the same input, and on MCP the caller's requested relation is silently discarded while a possible duplicate (T42 was named precisely because the record relates to it) is allowed through.

The new message logic infers the relation kind by probing per-kind keys on `out.data`:

```python
said = {"related": "related to", "duplicate_of": "duplicate of", "extends": "extends"}
linked = next((f" ({said[r]} {out.data[r]})" for r in said if out.data.get(r)), "")

```

instead of `(duplicate of D7)`. `"extends"` is dead as well for the same reason (extends is already intercepted by the `out.data.get("extended")` early return). chunk_findings.detail:
`_fit_sections` does not guarantee its result fits in `room`. `allow[i]` is `min(size_i, max(int(room * share), _SECTION_FLOOR))`, and because `_SECTION_FLOOR = 160` is a floor, `sum(allow)` can exceed `room` (the nine shares sum to 1.0, but four small-share sections get bumped up to 160). When that happens `slack = room - sum(allow)` is negative, the `while slack > 0` loop never runs, no allowance is ever reduced, and every section for which `size <= allow` is emitted in full while `trimmed` stays `False`. The budget is therefore silently exceeded exactly in the case this change is meant to police.

Concrete repro at the default budget converted to characters (room = 4800): section sizes of recovery 480, jobs 240, current 960, ready 576, decisions 1200, memories 384, rules 160, lessons 720, skills 160. Their sum is 4880 > 4800, so the early `sum(sizes) <= room` return does not fire. Each size equals its computed allowance (`decisions` 0.25*4800=1200, `rules` max(96,160)=160, `skills` max(144,160)=160, …), so `allow = sizes`, `sum(allow)=4880`, `slack=-80`; the loop is skipped, all sections satisfy `size <= room_i`, and the function returns 4880 characters with `trimmed=False`. A caller that trusts `trimmed` to add the "cut to fit" note will not add it, and the brief is 80 characters over budget. The error grows with smaller configured budgets: with room = 1000 the allowances sum to 1680 (`recovery`→160, `jobs`→160, `ready`→160, `memories`→160, `rules`→160, `skills`→160 vs. their 100–144 proportional shares), and a brief whose sections each sit at or below their allowance is returned essentially untrimmed (e.g. nine 150-character sections = 1350 characters against a 1000-character room, `trimmed=False`). The distribution loop assumes `sum(allow) < room`; whenever the floors push the sum over `room` it never trims anything and `trimmed` misreports the result.

Since `room` handed to `_fit_sections` already subtracts `len(note)`, the only circumstance in which the backstop can fire is the one the code's own comment acknowledges ("a heading alone overran its share"). In exactly that case, if the overrun `delta` is less than `len(note)` (~105 chars at the default token size), `len(text)` stays under `budget*4`, the check is False, `trimmed` is still True from `_fit_sections`, and `text += note` then pushes the result past the cap. The trigger must account for the note too (e.g. test after appending, or compare against `budget - len(note)//4`).

chunk_findings.detail: `_SECTION_FLOOR` is no longer a floor. The initial allowance is now `min(size, int(room * share))` for every section, and the floor is only topped up out of `slack = room - sum(allow)`. Whenever the sections still want their shares, `slack` is only the truncation remainder of `room * share` (at most ~1 char per section), while the shortfall for a section whose floor exceeds its share is `_SECTION_FLOOR - int(room * share)`. Concretely, with `room = 4000`, six sections sharing .35/.25/.20/.10/.05/.05 and `_SECTION_FLOOR = 300`: the two 5% sections are allowed `int(4000*0.05) = 200`, i.e. 100 chars under their floor, but `slack <= 6`, so the top-up loop (`extra = max(0, min(slack, min(size, _SECTION_FLOOR) - allow[i]))`) hands them a few characters at most and they are trimmed below the floor. If those sections are "rules"/"lessons", the trailing rule/lesson lines disappear — the exact failure this change is supposed to guarantee against. chunk_findings.detail: The test is titled and documented as covering the critic's regression — "shares first left the small sections under their floor whenever the big ones wanted their whole share" — but the inputs it builds cannot produce that situation. It constructs `sizes = [5001] * len(sections)`, i.e. every section demands exactly the same amount, and then calls `_allowances(sections, sizes, 2000)`. chunk_findings.detail:
Given input where the section is the jobs list with 15 exited-job records and its allowance is 5% of a 4800-character budget (`room_i ≈ 240`), the first entry line fails the fit test because `marker` already names all 15 omitted ids (~15 × 14 chars of ids plus separators ≈ 295 chars). The branch appends the marker unconditionally and returns, so the section's output is heading (≈21) + marker (≈295) ≈ 316 characters — larger than the `room_i = 240` it was told to fit, and larger than the total allowance the section was given. `_fit_sections` then reports `trimmed=True` without re-checking the total, so a brief whose other sections fill their shares ends up over `session.brief_max_tokens`. Because `named` grows with the number of omitted records, the overflow is unbounded: with 100 exited jobs the jobs section outputs ~1700 characters against a 240-character share, which is exactly the "a long section takes more than its budget" failure the change is meant to eliminate (and any downstream bottom-cut would then fall on the last sections, `lessons`/`skills`). The fix is to cap the named-id list (or the whole marker) to the remaining room, e.g. truncate `named`/`marker` before appending so the returned section is genuinely ≤ `room`.

Note also `heading` is kept even when `used + len(line) + 1 > room`, so a section can exceed its share by its heading length before the marker is even considered; this is smaller in magnitude but part of the same contract violation.

chunk_findings.detail: The test's stated purpose is that the agent's own job is listed ahead of other agents' running jobs, but it never creates a second running job for the ordering logic to outrank. The cross-kind refusal is suppressed with `chk = _cross_kind(repo, rule, agent, DD.Answer("new") if answer else None)`, i.e. on the mere truthiness of `answer`, but the docstring states the rule is filed "unless it reads like a record of another kind and nobody has answered `new`". Nothing here re-checks `answer.relation` (and, unlike `_points_elsewhere`, nothing re-checks `answer.problem`), so any non-`None` `RuleDedupAnswer` is turned into the user having said "new".

Concrete inputs:
- A problem-flagged answer (the CLI/MCP mis-parses an answer, e.g. `RuleDedupAnswer(relation="extend", target="rule-999", problem="unknown target")`). `_points_elsewhere` returns `False` because it guards on `not answer.problem`, execution falls through to `_add_checked_against_others`, `answer` is truthy, `DD.Answer("new")` is handed to `check_add`, no refusal is returned, and the rule is written to disk even though its text restates an existing decision — the very refusal the change is supposed to surface is silently skipped and the malformed answer is treated as approval.
- An answer whose `relation` is `"related"` but whose `target` is an existing *rule* (so `_points_elsewhere` is `False` via `not _is_rule`). Since the rule-level prompt is a separate check (`rule_dedup_check`, per `_cross_kind`'s docstring) the other-kind candidate was never shown to the user, yet `_add_checked_against_others` again substitutes `Answer("new")` and files the rule without ever running the decision/lesson/task comparison.

The suppression should be conditioned on `answer.relation == "new"` (and no `answer.problem`), not on `answer` being non-empty.

chunk_findings.detail: Given an environment where an existing rule R1 and an existing decision D are both similar to a new rule R2, the two entry points return different verdicts. `rule check R2` unconditionally invokes `_cross_kind`, merges D's candidate (kind "decision") and sets `would_ask=True`, even though the rule-vs-rule dedupe already produced `is_duplicate=True` with R1 as a candidate. `rule add R2` with no `dedup_answer` takes `is_duplicate=True`, so the new guard `not is_duplicate and (...)` is false, the cross-kind call is never made, and the add flow goes to the pre-existing rule-duplicate branch. The user answers "new" for R1; on re-entry `is_duplicate` is still true (R1 still exists) and `dedup_answer.relation == "new"` cannot rescue the guard because it also requires `not is_duplicate`, so `_add_checked_against_others` is never reached and D is never surfaced. The check therefore reports a candidate/would-ask that the add path can never produce (the inverse of the comment "as `rule add` would meet it"), and the D-rule-dedupe-everywhere goal is silently skipped for any rule that also duplicates another rule. Either the check should be gated on `not is_duplicate` to match add, or the add path's cross-kind check must also run in the rule-duplicate branch before finalizing a "new" answer; the two paths in this diff do not agree.

chunk_findings.detail: `rule_add` rejects an answer whose relation it does not recognise — the visible context line immediately above this hunk is `return O.failed("rule.added", f"Unknown relation: {dedup_answer.relation}", id=rule.id)`. The new edit path never performs that validation: it only special-cases `problem`, `extends` and `duplicate_of`, and then forwards everything else straight into `DD.Answer(dedup_answer.relation, dedup_answer.target)` and on into `_cross_kind`. So for an input such as `rule_update(repo, "RULE-1", title="Use UTC everywhere", dedup_answer=RuleDedupAnswer(relation="aaprove", target="DEC-2"))` (a typo, or a relation string an MCP client/agent generated), the guard is False, the refusal never fires, and the edit is neither rejected nor re-asked the way the identical answer is on `rule add`; depending on how `DD.Answer`/`_cross_kind` treat an unrecognised relation, the dedupe refusal is either bypassed (the edit proceeds with the answer never actually resolved) or it surfaces as an uncaught error from the `DD.Answer` construction instead of the clean `Unknown relation` failure that add produces. chunk_findings.detail: The `add` path was taught to handle the third dedupe answer ("extend"): when `rule_add` merges the rule text into an existing record it returns `extended`/`extended_kind` and the CLI prints `rule text added to <id> (<kind>); no rule <a.id> filed` instead of claiming a rule was filed. `_cmd_edit` implements only the "ask" branch (`out.exit != 0 and candidates`) and the "related" case; it never inspects `out.data.get("extended")`, and `_PAYLOADS["edit"]` was deliberately given `("id", "candidates", "related", "options")` with no `extended`/`extended_kind`, unlike the `add` tuple. So when a user runs, e.g. `ddflow rule edit R1 --extends D5 --content "..."` (or the MCP equivalent) and `rule_update` resolves the overlap by extending D5 rather than updating R1, `_cmd_edit` falls through to `f"updated {a.id}: ..."`, telling the user/MCP client that R1 was updated when the text was actually moved into the decision/lesson, and the `extended` fields are stripped from the JSON payload. chunk_findings.detail: The MCP edit tool resolves the dedup answer with `RuleDedupAnswer("new", "") if bool(a.get("new")) else (RuleDedupAnswer("related", a["related"]) if a.get("related") else None)`. There is no schema-level exclusivity: `"new": ("boolean", ...)` and `"related": ("string", ...)` are declared as independent optional properties, and the schema format used here cannot express "at most one of". So a client that sends `{"id": "R1", "content": "...", "new": true, "related": "T42"}` (legal under the declared schema) silently gets `RuleDedupAnswer("new", "")`: the explicit `related` answer is dropped and the edit is treated as a brand-new record. The equivalent CLI invocation `rule edit --new --related T42` fails with an argparse "not allowed with argument" error, so the two surfaces disagree on the same input, and on MCP the caller's requested relation is silently discarded while a possible duplicate (T42 was named precisely because the record relates to it) is allowed through.

chunk_findings.detail:
The new message logic infers the relation kind by probing per-kind keys on `out.data`:

```python
said = {"related": "related to", "duplicate_of": "duplicate of", "extends": "extends"}
linked = next((f" ({said[r]} {out.data[r]})" for r in said if out.data.get(r)), "")
```

But the result object does not carry those keys. For a link, the target id is `out.data["related"]` and the *kind* is `out.data["relation"]` — that is exactly why this same diff adds `"relation"` to `_PAYLOADS["add"]`, and it mirrors the `extended` / `extended_kind` pair used a few lines above (id + kind). So the probe `out.data.get("duplicate_of")` never matches, the first dict key `"related"` matches instead (the id is present), and the CLI prints the wrong phrase: after `ddflow rule add --id r1 --title T --content C` and answering the dedupe prompt with the **duplicate_of** option, the user sees

```
added rule r1 (related to D7)
```

instead of `(duplicate of D7)`. `"extends"` is dead as well for the same reason (extends is already intercepted by the `out.data.get("extended")` early return). The phrase should be derived from `out.data.get("relation")` with the id from `out.data.get("related")`. `_cmd_edit` has the same root cause from the other direction: it unconditionally hard-codes `f" (related to {related})"`, so an edit resolved with the duplicate_of answer is also reported as "related to".

chunk_findings.detail:
The new helper short-circuits the whole dedupe check whenever the answer's target is an existing rule:

```python
related = {"related": answer.target} if answer and answer.relation == "related" else {}
if answer is not None and answer.target and _is_rule(repo, answer.target):
    return None, related
```

This means `_cross_kind` is never invoked on that path, so neither `chk.refusal` nor `chk.data()` (candidates / `dedupe_unavailable`) is produced. The change's stated purpose is that a rule edit "runs the same check_add against decisions, lessons, research and tasks"; a rule target is now itself one of the compared kinds (`'rule' in [dedupe].kinds`), so `_cross_kind` is capable of resolving a rule-target answer and still reporting candidates from the *other* kinds. Skipping it loses those.

Concrete failing input: rule `r-1` currently holds content `Y`; a decision `d-1` holds content `X`; rule `r-2` exists. Run an edit that sets `r-1`'s content to `X` and supplies the answer `{relation: "related", target: "r-2"}`. Because `_is_rule(repo, "r-2")` is true, the helper returns `(None, {"related": "r-2"})` without running `_cross_kind`, so `rule_update` succeeds and the outcome contains no `candidates` entry for `d-1`. The rule now silently restates decision `d-1`, which is exactly the case the change is supposed to catch; the same edit with the answer `{relation: "new"}` or `{relation: "related", target: "d-1"}` *does* run the check and surfaces `d-1`.

chunk_findings.detail: `_check_note` drops every candidate whose kind is `"rule"`, so a rule that duplicates another rule is silently un-warned. Scenario: edit rule `R1` so its text is near-identical to the existing rule `R2`. chunk_findings.detail: `_caller` consults `params._meta` first and, if the metadata name is unusable, returns immediately without ever examining the `as_agent` argument. That contradicts the precedence this same diff announces twice: the README says "the argument wins when both are given", and `_caller`'s own docstring says the `as_agent` argument "wins over both". Concrete input: a modern request with `params = {"name": "ddflow_status", "arguments": {"as_agent": "bob"}, "_meta": {"ddflow/agent": "not a name!"}}`. `_meta_agent(params)` yields `("not a name!", "<reason>")`, so line 512 returns `(self.agent, "", args, "<reason>")` and the call is rejected with "'not a name!' is not a usable agent name", even though the caller supplied a perfectly valid per-call name that is documented to take precedence. The precedence only holds when the `_meta` name is *also* valid, which is the one case where it does not matter. The same early return is also the only error path that hands back `args` still containing `as_agent` (the `_meta` value is never popped), so the returned arguments are inconsistent with the "arguments without `as_agent`" contract the function documents.

chunk_findings.detail: The reordering makes `_meta` validation conditional on `as_agent` being absent. In the old code `_meta_agent(params)` was read and its `bad` result returned *before* `as_agent` was examined, so a request carrying a malformed `params._meta["ddflow/agent"]` was rejected no matter what else it carried (fail-closed). In the new code, when `AS_AGENT` is present with a valid non-empty value, the function returns at `if want: return want, want, args, ""` without ever calling `_meta_agent`, so the malformed `_meta` name is silently discarded. Concrete input: on a modern (2026-07-28) connection, `args = {"as_agent": "bob"}` and `params._meta = {"ddflow/agent": "not a name!"}`. Old code returns `(self.agent, "", args, "<malformed-name error>")`; new code returns `("bob", "bob", args, "")` and the tool executes as `bob`. That contradicts the protocol rule this same change documents: the README paragraph right above the edited text still states "the argument wins when both are given; a malformed name is a tool error" — the argument winning should select which name is used, not suppress the documented error for a malformed name that is present in the request. If the intended contract really is "an explicit `as_agent` makes `_meta` unread", then the README sentence needs to say so, and the test for `_meta` naming needs a companion case (`as_agent` present + malformed `_meta`) to pin the behavior; as written, doc and code disagree.
